--- title: "Tutorial: Using the emmeans R Package" date: "1/6/2025" date-modified: last-modified date-format: long --- # Emmeans Tutorial ## 1. Introduction ### Overview `emmeans` (Estimated Marginal Means) is an R package designed for the analysis of linear models. It provides tools for obtaining and visualizing adjusted means for factors in statistical models, allowing users to interpret complex model outputs more easily. ### Use Cases - **Post-hoc Comparisons:** Evaluating differences between group means after fitting a model. - **Visualization:** Creating clear and informative plots of marginal means. - **Model Checking:** Assessing the fit and assumptions of linear models. ### Benefits - Simplifies the interpretation of model outputs. - Facilitates the comparison of means across different factors. - Integrates seamlessly with various types of models in R. ## 2. Getting Started ### Loading the Package First, load the `emmeans` package into your R session: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(emmeans) ``` ::: ### Basic Usage Here's a simple example using a linear model: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sample data data(mtcars) # Fit a linear model model <- lm(mpg ~ factor(cyl), data = mtcars) # Obtain estimated marginal means emm <- emmeans(model, ~cyl) summary(emm) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| cyl| emmean| SE| df| lower.CL| upper.CL| |---:|--------:|---------:|--:|--------:|--------:| | 4| 26.66364| 0.9718008| 29| 24.67608| 28.65119| | 6| 19.74286| 1.2182168| 29| 17.25132| 22.23439| | 8| 15.10000| 0.8614094| 29| 13.33822| 16.86178|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} tapply(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$cyl, mean) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4 6 8 26.66364 19.74286 15.10000 ``` ::: ::: *Annotation:* This will provide the estimated marginal means of miles per gallon (mpg) adjusted for the number of cylinders (cyl). ## 3. Key Functions and Features ### `emmeans()` - **Description:** Computes estimated marginal means for specified factors in a model. - **Syntax:** ```r emmeans(object, specs, ...) ``` - `object`: A fitted model object. - `specs`: Terms for which to compute marginal means. - **Example:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Example of emmeans emm_cyl <- emmeans(model, ~cyl) print(emm_cyl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` cyl emmean SE df lower.CL upper.CL 4 26.7 0.972 29 24.7 28.7 6 19.7 1.220 29 17.3 22.2 8 15.1 0.861 29 13.3 16.9 Confidence level used: 0.95 ``` ::: ::: *This will display the estimated marginal means for each cylinder category.* ### `pairs()` - **Description:** Computes pairwise comparisons among estimated marginal means. - **Syntax:** ```r pairs(x, ...) ``` - `x`: An object of class `emmeans`. - **Example:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pairwise comparisons pairs(emm_cyl) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value cyl4 - cyl6 6.92 1.56 29 4.441 0.0003 cyl4 - cyl8 11.56 1.30 29 8.905 <.0001 cyl6 - cyl8 4.64 1.49 29 3.112 0.0112 P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates ``` ::: ::: *This gives pairwise comparisons between the cylinder levels.* ## 4. In-Depth Examples ### Title: Comparing MPG Across Cylinder Counts #### Objective To evaluate how the number of cylinders affects the miles per gallon (mpg) in cars. #### Steps 1. **Data Preparation:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data(mtcars) model <- lm(mpg ~ factor(cyl), data = mtcars) ``` ::: 2. **Function Application:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emm_cyl <- emmeans(model, ~cyl) ``` ::: 3. **Visualization:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(emm_cyl) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans-v1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 4. **Output:** The plot will show the estimated marginal means of mpg for each cylinder group, allowing for quick visual comparisons. ## 5. Advanced Features ### Customization You can customize the output of `emmeans` using additional arguments: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emm_cyl <- emmeans(model, ~cyl, at = list(cyl = c(4, 6, 8))) ``` ::: ### Integration `emmeans` can be used with packages like `ggplot2` for enhanced visualizations: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) emm_df <- as.data.frame(emm_cyl) ggplot(emm_df, aes(x = cyl, y = emmean)) + geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower.CL, ymax = upper.CL)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans-v1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 6. Troubleshooting and FAQs ### Common Issues - **Error: Object not found**: Ensure the model object exists and is correctly specified. - **Warnings about convergence**: Check the model fitting process for issues related to data or model complexity. ### FAQs - **Q:** Can `emmeans` be used with non-linear models? - **A:** Yes, `emmeans` supports various model types, including generalized linear models. ## 7. Best Practices - Use clear and descriptive variable names when fitting models. - Regularly check model diagnostics to ensure assumptions are met. - Document your analysis steps for reproducibility. ## 8. Conclusion ### Summary In this tutorial, we explored the `emmeans` package, covering its key functions, in-depth examples, and advanced features. ### Next Steps Try applying `emmeans` to your own datasets or explore more advanced statistical models. ### Encouragement Dive into your data analysis projects with confidence, utilizing the power of `emmeans`! ## 9. References and Resources - **Documentation:** [emmeans Documentation](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/emmeans/emmeans.pdf) - **Learning Materials:** [R for Data Science](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/) - **Support Channels:** [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/rvlenth/emmeans/issues), [Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/emmeans) ```{mermaid} graph TD; A[Start] --> B[Load Package]; B --> C[Fit Model]; C --> D[Compute EMM]; D --> E[Visualize Results]; E --> F[Interpret Output]; F --> G[Explore Further]; G --> H[End]; ``` --- # Handling Interactions with `emmeans` When working with linear models that include interaction terms, `emmeans` allows you to explore and visualize these interactions effectively. Here's how to manage interactions using the `emmeans` package. ## 1. Understanding Interactions Interactions occur when the effect of one predictor variable on the response variable depends on the level of another predictor. For example, the relationship between treatment and outcome may vary depending on gender. ## 2. Fitting a Model with Interactions ### Example Let's create a model with an interaction between two factors, `treatment` and `gender`, on the response variable `outcome`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Sample data data(mtcars) # Create a categorical variable for the example mtcars$am <- factor(mtcars$am, labels = c("Automatic", "Manual")) # Fit a linear model with interaction model <- lm(mpg ~ am * cyl, data = mtcars) ``` ::: ## 3. Using `emmeans` for Interactions ### Compute Estimated Marginal Means To compute estimated marginal means for the interaction, use the `emmeans()` function with the interaction term specified. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Obtain estimated marginal means for the interaction emm_interaction <- emmeans(model, ~ am * cyl) summary(emm_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|am | cyl| emmean| SE| df| lower.CL| upper.CL| |:---------|------:|--------:|--------:|--:|--------:|--------:| |Automatic | 6.1875| 18.64867| 0.755581| 28| 17.10093| 20.19640| |Manual | 6.1875| 20.74867| 1.016399| 28| 18.66667| 22.83067|
::: ::: ### Interpret the Output The output will give you the estimated marginal means for each combination of the levels of `am` and `cyl`. This allows for examining how the means differ based on the interaction. ## 4. Visualizing Interactions Visualizing interactions can help in understanding how the effects vary. Use the `plot()` function to create interaction plots. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Interaction plot plot(emm_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans-v1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Customizing the Plot You can further customize the plot using `ggplot2` for enhanced visual representation: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) # Convert emmeans object to a data frame emm_df <- as.data.frame(emm_interaction) # Create a ggplot ggplot(emm_df, aes(x = cyl, y = emmean, color = am)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + labs( title = "Interaction between Treatment and Cylinder", x = "Number of Cylinders", y = "Estimated Marginal Mean MPG" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans-v1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 5. Pairwise Comparisons You can also perform pairwise comparisons for the interaction effects: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Pairwise comparisons for the interaction pairs(emm_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` contrast estimate SE df t.ratio p.value Automatic cyl6.1875 - Manual cyl6.1875 -2.1 1.27 28 -1.658 0.1085 ``` ::: ::: This will give you insights into which combinations of `am` and `cyl` are significantly different from one another. ## Conclusion Handling interactions in `emmeans` is straightforward and provides valuable insights into how different factors influence the response variable. By fitting models that include interactions, computing estimated marginal means, and visualizing the results, you can effectively interpret complex relationships in your data. --- # Handling Interactions with More Than Two Factors in `emmeans` When dealing with interactions involving multiple factors, `emmeans` can help you explore and visualize these complex relationships. Here's a guide on how to manage interactions with more than two factors using the `emmeans` package. ## 1. Understanding Multi-Factor Interactions Multi-factor interactions occur when the effect of one factor on the response variable depends on the levels of two or more other factors. For example, you may want to investigate how the effect of treatment varies across different levels of gender and age group. ## 2. Fitting a Model with Multiple Interactions ### Example Let's create a hypothetical dataset and fit a model that includes interactions among three factors: `treatment`, `gender`, and `age_group`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Load necessary library library(dplyr) # Simulated dataset set.seed(123) data <- data.frame( treatment = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 30)), gender = factor(rep(c("Male", "Female"), times = 30)), age_group = factor(rep(c("Young", "Old"), each = 15, times = 2)), outcome = rnorm(60, 50, 10) ) # Fit a linear model with interactions model <- lm(outcome ~ treatment * gender * age_group, data = data) ``` ::: ## 3. Using `emmeans` for Multi-Factor Interactions ### Compute Estimated Marginal Means To compute estimated marginal means for the interaction among the three factors, specify the interaction in the `emmeans()` function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Obtain estimated marginal means for the interaction emm_multi <- emmeans(model, ~ treatment * gender * age_group) summary(emm_multi) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|treatment |gender |age_group | emmean| SE| df| lower.CL| upper.CL| |:---------|:------|:---------|--------:|--------:|--:|--------:|--------:| |A |Female |Old | 47.65142| 3.312310| 52| 41.00478| 54.29805| |B |Female |Old | 52.47994| 3.312310| 52| 45.83330| 59.12657| |A |Male |Old | 47.39998| 3.541008| 52| 40.29443| 54.50554| |B |Male |Old | 48.48123| 3.541008| 52| 41.37567| 55.58678| |A |Female |Young | 50.45024| 3.541008| 52| 43.34469| 57.55579| |B |Female |Young | 53.98623| 3.541008| 52| 46.88067| 61.09178| |A |Male |Young | 52.46324| 3.312310| 52| 45.81661| 59.10988| |B |Male |Young | 52.04873| 3.312310| 52| 45.40209| 58.69537|
::: ::: ### Interpret the Output The output will display the estimated marginal means for each combination of the levels of `treatment`, `gender`, and `age_group`. This helps you understand how the outcome varies across these groups. ## 4. Visualizing Multi-Factor Interactions Visualizing interactions with multiple factors can be complex, but it can be done effectively using `ggplot2`. Here's how to create a plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) # Convert emmeans object to a data frame emm_df <- as.data.frame(emm_multi) # Create a ggplot ggplot(emm_df, aes(x = treatment, y = emmean, group = interaction(gender, age_group), color = interaction(gender, age_group))) + geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) + geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) + labs( title = "Multi-Factor Interaction", x = "Treatment", y = "Estimated Marginal Mean Outcome" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans-v1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Customizing the Plot You can adjust the aesthetics of the plot to improve clarity, such as adding `facet_wrap()` to separate plots by one of the factors: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(emm_df, aes(x = treatment, y = emmean, color = gender)) + geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) + geom_line(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), aes(group = age_group)) + facet_wrap(~age_group) + labs( title = "Multi-Factor Interaction by Age Group", x = "Treatment", y = "Estimated Marginal Mean Outcome" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](emmeans-v1_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## 5.
